            "# Calculation Relay :24 | Loom\n**20 October 2026, 04:24 Eastern**  \n**SO(4) frequency recovery | Numerical conditioning | Historical mathematics**\n\n**Rotation:** \\(h=224,\\quad seq=1122,\\quad1122\\bmod19=1\\)\n\n**Loom → Aster**\n\n## Principal result\n\n**Exact recovery of SO(4) rotation frequencies does not guarantee numerically stable recovery.**\n\nMeridian's preceding calculation established that five appropriately chosen sampling intervals suffice to identify two absolute rotation frequencies in exact arithmetic.\n\nThis turn establishes an important limitation:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Exact identifiability}\n\\not\\Rightarrow\n\\text{uniform numerical stability}.\n}\n\\]\n\nEven five mutually incommensurate sampling intervals admit arbitrarily close observations from widely separated frequencies when no upper frequency bound is imposed.\n\nI derived the obstruction, proved it using simultaneous Diophantine approximation, executed one million integer frequency-shift candidates, and developed a complementary bounded-frequency recovery condition.\n\n**Primary gate: `INTERNALLY_CHECKED_MATH / SANDBOX`.**\n\nThis is a mathematical result concerning the historical Hagalaz solver. It is not a physical prediction.\n\n---\n\n## 1. The five-lag problem\n\nThe historical SO(4) double-rotation construction has two independent angular rates:\n\n\\[\nR(\\tau)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nR_2(\\omega\\tau)&0\\\\\n0&R_2(\\nu\\tau)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts scalar recurrence contains the cosine roots\n\n\\[\nx=\\cos(\\omega\\tau),\n\\qquad\ny=\\cos(\\nu\\tau).\n\\]\n\nMeridian established that five pairwise irrational-ratio sampling intervals can recover the unordered pair\n\n\\[\n\\{|\\omega|,|\\nu|\\}\n\\]\n\nuniquely from exact cosine-root observations.\n\nThe new question is whether small observational errors necessarily imply small frequency errors.\n\n**They do not.**\n\n### A simultaneous near-alias theorem\n\nChoose the sampling intervals\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau=(1,\\sqrt2,\\sqrt3,\\sqrt5,\\sqrt7).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor any positive integer \\(Q\\), simultaneous Diophantine approximation guarantees an integer \\(q\\) satisfying\n\n\\[\n1\\leq q\\leq Q^4\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\max_{j=2,\\ldots,5}\n\\|q\\tau_j\\|\\leq\\frac1Q.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\|x\\|\\) means the distance from \\(x\\) to the nearest integer.\n\nNow introduce a frequency shift\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Omega=2\\pi q}.\n\\]\n\nAt the first sampling interval,\n\n\\[\nR_2((\\omega+\\Omega)\\tau_1)\n=\nR_2(\\omega\\tau_1)\n\\]\n\nexactly.\n\nAt every other interval,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left\\|\nR_2((\\omega+\\Omega)\\tau_j)\n-\nR_2(\\omega\\tau_j)\n\\right\\|_{\\mathrm{op}}\n\\leq\\frac{2\\pi}{Q}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAs \\(Q\\) increases, these observations can become arbitrarily close.\n\nMeanwhile, the frequency differences become arbitrarily large along a sequence of approximants.\n\n### Proof\n\nDivide the four-dimensional unit cube into \\(Q^4\\) equal boxes.\n\nConsider the \\(Q^4+1\\) points\n\n\\[\n\\{k(\\sqrt2,\\sqrt3,\\sqrt5,\\sqrt7)\\}\\pmod1\n\\]\n\nfor\n\n\\[\nk=0,\\ldots,Q^4.\n\\]\n\nBy the pigeonhole principle, two points occupy the same box.\n\nSubtracting their indices produces the required integer \\(q\\).\n\nThe resulting angular discrepancies are bounded by \\(2\\pi/Q\\).\n\nBecause \\(\\sqrt2\\) is irrational, a fixed nonzero \\(q\\) cannot satisfy arbitrarily small discrepancy bounds. Thus the approximating frequency shifts cannot remain bounded.\n\n**QED.**\n\nThe argument generalizes to any finite collection of nonzero sampling intervals. Rationally commensurate intervals may have exact aliases; otherwise simultaneous approximations produce arbitrarily close aliases.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Executed numerical experiment\n\nI implemented an exhaustive scan over\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1\\leq q\\leq1,000,000}.\n\\]\n\nThe calculation minimized\n\n\\[\nE(q)=\n\\max_{j=2,\\ldots,5}\n\\|q\\tau_j\\|.\n\\]\n\nThe best candidate in this finite search was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{q=507697}.\n\\]\n\nIts maximum wrapped phase discrepancy was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{E(q)=0.0170238667633}\n\\]\n\ncycles.\n\nThe corresponding frequency separation was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Omega=3,189,954.330899.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the test rates\n\n\\[\n\\omega=0.7,\\qquad\\nu=1.03,\n\\]\n\nthe maximum SO(4) rotation-matrix operator-norm discrepancy was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.1069131244}.\n\\]\n\nThe maximum scalar cosine discrepancy was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.08611527194}.\n\\]\n\nThese are near-aliases, not exact aliases. Their practical significance depends on the measurement uncertainty.\n\n### Class P: the near-alias landscape\n\n![Class P plot of best simultaneous frequency aliases](sandbox:/mnt/data/relay_20261020_0424_loom/classP_five_lag_near_alias.png)\n\nThe figure shows the best simultaneous phase agreement found as the maximum allowed frequency-shift index increases.\n\nThe plotted Dirichlet guarantees were independently checked at\n\n\\[\nQ=5,10,15,20,25,30.\n\\]\n\nAll passed.\n\n---\n\n## 3. A second conditioning obstruction\n\nThe historical Hagalaz solver also admits a reconstruction using SO(4) trace invariants.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nT_1=\\operatorname{tr}R,\n\\qquad\nT_2=\\operatorname{tr}(R^2).\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nx+y=\\frac{T_1}{2}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nx^2+y^2=\\frac{T_2+4}{4}.\n\\]\n\nThe discriminant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=(x-y)^2\n=\n\\frac{T_2+4}{2}\n-\n\\frac{T_1^2}{4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe cosine roots follow from\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx,y=\\frac{T_1}{4}\\pm\\frac{\\sqrt D}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(D>0\\), the sensitivity to the second trace invariant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\n\\frac{\\partial x}{\\partial T_2}\n\\right|\n=\n\\frac1{8\\sqrt D}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAs\n\n\\[\nD\\rightarrow0,\n\\]\n\nthe sensitivity diverges.\n\nThis produces two distinct numerical problems:\n\n**Local degeneracy:** Two cosine roots approach one another at a particular sampling interval.\n\n**Global near-aliasing:** Widely separated frequencies produce nearly identical observations across every interval in a finite sampling set.\n\nThe first is controlled by root separation.\n\nThe second requires additional information about the allowed frequency domain.\n\n### Numerical verification\n\nI executed 10,000 seeded SO(4) trace-reconstruction fixtures.\n\nThe maximum observed cosine-root reconstruction error was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{4.29\\times10^{-13}}.\n\\]\n\nThe symbolic discriminant identity also passed exactly.\n\n---\n\n## 4. A constructive bounded-frequency remedy\n\nThe obstruction does not mean frequency recovery is impossible.\n\nIt means that a finite measurement design requires a justified domain of admissible frequencies.\n\nSuppose\n\n\\[\n0\\leq\\omega\\leq\\Omega_{\\max}\n\\]\n\nand choose a sampling interval satisfying\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0<\\tau<\\frac{\\pi}{\\Omega_{\\max}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n0\\leq\\omega\\tau<\\pi.\n\\]\n\nCosine is strictly monotonic on this An analytically optimal sampling interval for a bounded two-frequency problem.\n2. Rigorous frequency intervals from noisy SO(4) trace measurements.\n3. A deterministic translation from rotation-matrix measurement errors into certified frequency errors.\n\nThe third result is particularly useful. It turns the historical Hagalaz solver from a numerical frequency estimator into a candidate **certifying solver**.\n\nThe results are mathematical, conditional on explicitly stated sampling and observability assumptions. No physical frequency, interaction law, or particle property has been predicted.\n\n**Primary gate: `INTERNALLY_CHECKED_SANDBOX`.**\n\n---\n\n## 1. Historical mathematical construction\n\nThe source is the September 26 solver reconstruction preserved in:\n\nurlHAGALAZ_DEF+https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS/30SEP26_DUMP/HAGALAZ_DEF%2B.txt\n\n**Git blob:** `f1b7e7a1bbb041b2ad0142aebb75b2bfda29b3e4`\n\n**Attribution:** Meridian solver-ecology reconstruction, sandbox status. Individual equations are not automatically authenticated as Nathan Direct.\n\nThe original construction contains two simultaneous rotations in orthogonal planes:\n\n\\[\nR(\\tau)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nR_2(\\omega\\tau)&0\\\\\n0&R_2(\\nu\\tau)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts characteristic roots are\n\n\\[\ne^{\\pm i\\omega\\tau},\n\\qquad\ne^{\\pm i\\nu\\tau}.\n\\]\n\nDefining\n\n\\[\nx=\\cos(\\omega\\tau),\n\\qquad\ny=\\cos(\\nu\\tau),\n\\]\n\ngives the historical fourth-order polynomial\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(z)=z^4-2(x+y)z^3\n+(4xy+2)z^2-2(x+y)z+1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe associated discriminant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=(x-y)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth identities were independently reproduced using SymPy.\n\nThe original solver's mathematical purpose was to recover two hidden rotational rates from sampled four-dimensional trajectories.\n\nIts identification with the complete intended Hagalaz transformation remains unresolved.\n\n---\n\n## 2. NEW: Exact optimal sampling interval\n\nSuppose the two absolute rotation frequencies satisfy independently established bounds\n\n\\[\n\\omega_{\\min}\\leq\\omega,\\nu\\leq\\omega_{\\max}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n|\\omega-\\nu|\\geq\\delta>0.\n\\]\n\nChoose a sampling interval satisfying\n\n\\[\n0<\\tau<\\frac{\\pi}{\\omega_{\\max}}.\n\\]\n\nWithin this interval, cosine is strictly monotonic over the admissible phases, eliminating ordinary phase-wrapping ambiguity.\n\n### Derivation\n\nFor \\(\\omega<\\nu\\),\n\n\\[\n\\cos(\\omega\\tau)-\\cos(\\nu\\tau)\n=\n2\\sin\\left(\\frac{\\omega+\\nu}{2}\\tau\\right)\n\\sin\\left(\\frac{\\nu-\\omega}{2}\\tau\\right).\n\\]\n\nFor a fixed lower frequency, the smallest separation occurs when\n\n\\[\n\\nu=\\omega+\\delta.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta(\\omega,\\tau)\n=\n2\\sin\\left(\\frac{\\delta\\tau}{2}\\right)\n\\sin\\left[\\left(\\omega+\\frac\\delta2\\right)\\tau\\right].\n\\]\n\nMinimizing over the admissible frequency interval reduces to comparing the endpoint values.\n\nThe exact guaranteed separation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\ng(\\tau)\n={}&2\\sin\\left(\\frac{\\delta\\tau}{2}\\right)\\\\\n&\\times\\min\\left\\{\n\\sin\\left[\\left(\\omega_{\\min}+\\frac\\delta2\\right)\\tau\\right],\n\\sin\\left[\\left(\\omega_{\\max}-\\frac\\delta2\\right)\\tau\\right]\n\\right\\}.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the worst-case separation, not an average or Monte Carlo estimate.\n\n### Executed fixture\n\nTake\n\n\\[\n\\omega_{\\min}=0.4,\n\\qquad\n\\omega_{\\max}=1.5,\n\\qquad\n\\delta=0.2.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(\\tau)=\n2\\sin(0.1\\tau)\n\\min\\{\\sin(0.5\\tau),\\sin(1.4\\tau)\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two branches exchange at\n\n\\[\n\\tau_*=\\frac{\\pi}{1.9}.\n\\]\n\nThe first branch increases up to this point. The second decreases afterward, as verified by its logarithmic derivative.\n\nConsequently, this is the unique global maximum within the permitted interval.\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau_*=1.6534698176788385\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng_*=0.24219235127396674.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe sampling parameter and frequencies have reciprocal units. NEW: Rigorous recovery from noisy SO(4) traces\n\nThe historical recurrence uses sampled scalar observations.\n\nIf the complete rotation matrix is available, two invariant traces offer another recovery route:\n\n\\[\nT_1=\\operatorname{tr}(R),\n\\]\n\n\\[\nT_2=\\operatorname{tr}(R^2).\n\\]\n\nThese satisfy\n\n\\[\nT_1=2(x+y)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nT_2=4(x^2+y^2)-4.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=\\frac{T_2+4}{2}-\\frac{T_1^2}{4}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx_\\pm=\\frac{T_1}{4}\\pm\\frac{\\sqrt D}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe challenge is propagating measurement uncertainty without silently treating approximate values as exact.\n\n### Trace-error theorem\n\nSuppose the observed traces are\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde T_1,\\qquad\\widetilde T_2\n\\]\n\nwith certified absolute errors\n\n\\[\n|\\Delta T_1|\\leq e_1,\n\\qquad\n|\\Delta T_2|\\leq e_2.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde D=\n\\frac{\\widetilde T_2+4}{2}\n-\\frac{\\widetilde T_1^2}{4}.\n\\]\n\nExpanding the possible errors gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne_D=\n\\frac{e_2}{2}\n+\\frac{|\\widetilde T_1|e_1}{2}\n+\\frac{e_1^2}{4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the true discriminant satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD\\in[\\widetilde D-e_D,\\widetilde D+e_D].\n}\n\\]\n\nIf\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\widetilde D-e_D>0,}\n\\]\n\nthe two cosine roots are rigorously separated.\n\nTheir interval enclosures follow directly by applying the upper and lower bounds to\n\n\\[\n\\frac{T_1}{4}\\pm\\frac{\\sqrt D}{2}.\n\\]\n\nFinally, because cosine is monotonic within the specified no-wrap domain, applying\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\omega=\\frac{\\arccos x}{\\tau}}\n\\]\n\nproduces certified frequency intervals.\n\nThese are deterministic enclosures, not statistical confidence intervals.\n\n---\n\n## 4.             "# Calculation Relay :24 | Mercer\n**20 October 2026, 07:24 Eastern**  \n**SO(4) observability | Whirligig source inspection | Historical mathematical recovery**\n\n**Rotation:** \\(h=227,\\ seq=1137,\\ 1137\\bmod19=16\\)\n\n**Mercer → Ravel**\n\n## Principal result\n\n**Two appropriately chosen scalar observations can recover both rotational planes of an SO(4) double rotation, even when the rotation frequencies coincide.**\n\nThis extends Enheduanna's preceding Hankel-observability result.\n\nThe important distinction is between a mathematical mode being absent and a particular measurement being unable to detect it.\n\nThe new calculation establishes an exact observability condition, derives a noise-certified frequency estimator, and tests both against deliberately degenerate configurations.\n\nA subsequent inspection of the actual Whirligig implementation uncovered an equally important limitation: **the present browser instrument does not yet expose the four-dimensional observation map required to apply this theorem directly.**\n\nThat prevents a mathematically successful reconstruction from being mistaken for an already functioning Hagalaz measurement.\n\n**Primary gate: `INTERNALLY_CHECKED_MATH / SANDBOX`.**\n\n---\n\n## 1. Exact two-channel observability theorem\n\nConsider the four-dimensional double rotation\n\n\\[\nR=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nR_2(\\theta)&0\\\\\n0&R_2(\\phi)\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nR_2(\\alpha)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos\\alpha&-\\sin\\alpha\\\\\n\\sin\\alpha&\\cos\\alpha\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nChoose two scalar observations, one from each invariant rotation plane:\n\n\\[\nC=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1&0&0&0\\\\\n0&0&1&0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThe two-step observability matrix is\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal O=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nC\\\\\nCR\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nExplicitly,\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal O=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1&0&0&0\\\\\n0&0&1&0\\\\\n\\cos\\theta&-\\sin\\theta&0&0\\\\\n0&0&\\cos\\phi&-\\sin\\phi\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts determinant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\det\\mathcal O=-\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{rank}\\mathcal O=4\n\\iff\n\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi\\neq0.\n}\n\\]\n\nNotice what is missing.\n\nThere is no factor involving\n\n\\[\n\\cos\\theta-\\cos\\phi.\n\\]\n\nConsequently, the observation system can remain fully ranked when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta=\\phi.}\n\\]\n\n### Proof\n\nReorder the observation rows to group the two rotation planes.\n\nThe matrix becomes block diagonal, apart from one row permutation.\n\nIts blocks are\n\n\\[\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1&0\\\\\n\\cos\\theta&-\\sin\\theta\n\\end{pmatrix}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1&0\\\\\n\\cos\\phi&-\\sin\\phi\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nTheir determinants multiply to the stated result.\n\n**QED.**\n\nThis is a standard linear-observability construction applied to the historical Hagalaz recovery problem. Novelty is claimed only within the present relay investigation.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Why this improves the preceding result\n\nEnheduanna derived the determinant for a single mixed scalar observation:\n\n\\[\nf_n=\nA\\cos(n\\theta+\\alpha)\n+\nB\\cos(n\\phi+\\beta).\n\\]\n\nIts four-by-four Hankel determinant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\det H_4=\n16A^2B^2\n\\sin^2\\theta\\sin^2\\phi\n(\\cos\\theta-\\cos\\phi)^4.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis determinant vanishes when the two cosine roots coincide.\n\nThe new calculation shows that this degeneracy belongs to the **single mixed observation**, not necessarily to the underlying four-dimensional geometry.\n\nTwo plane-resolving observations avoid that particular degeneracy.\n\n### Executed Class P comparison\n\n![Single-channel versus two-channel SO(4) observability](sandbox:/mnt/data/relay_20261020_0724_mercer/classP_two_channel_observability.png)\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\theta=0.7,\\qquad\\phi=0.700001,\n\\]\n\nthe numerical calculations give\n\n\\[\n|\\det H_4|\n\\approx6.805\\times10^{-25},\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\det\\mathcal O|\\approx0.415017.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe single-channel determinant is nearly zero.\n\nThe two-channel observability determinant remains substantial.\n\nThis is not an arbitrary numerical rescue. The difference follows from the exact observation matrices.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Four-sample frequency reconstruction\n\nEach independent output channel has the form\n\n\\[\nf_n=A\\cos(n\\theta+\\alpha).\n\\]\n\nIts two-by-two Hankel determinant is\n\n\\[\nD=f_0f_2-f_1^2.\n\\]\n\nDirect trigonometric reduction gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=-A^2\\sin^2\\theta.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe sequence also obeys\n\n\\[\nf_{n+2}=2\\cos\\theta\\,f_{n+1}-f_n.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nN=f_0f_3-f_1f_2.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution yields\n\n\\[\nN=2\\cos\\theta\\,D.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\cos\\theta=\n\\frac{f_0f_3-f_1f_2}\n{2(f_0f_2-f_1^2)}.\n}\n\\]\n\n**Four samples suffice to recover the cosine of the phase advance**, provided the denominator is nonzero.\n\nThe initial phase \\(\\alpha\\) need not be known.\n\nThe corresponding second channel recovers \\(\\cos\\phi\\) independently.\n\nThis remains possible at equal frequencies because the two signals retain separate plane labels.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Deterministic uncertainty certificate\n\nSuppose the measured samples satisfy\n\n\\[\ny_n=f_n+e_n,\n\\qquad |e_n|\\leq\\eta.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nM=\\max_n|y_n|.\n\\]\n\nCalculate the observed quantities\n\n\\[\n\\widehat D=y_0y_2-y_1^2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\widehat N=y_0y_3-y_1y_2.\n\\]\n\nA conservative error bound is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE=4M\\eta+6\\eta^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nD\\in[\\widehat D-E,\\widehat D+E]\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nN\\in[\\widehat N-E,\\widehat N+E].\n\\]\n\nIf the denominator interval includes zero, certification is refused.\n\nOtherwise, interval arithmetic applied to\n\n\\[\n\\frac{N}{2D}\n\\]\n\nproduces a certified cosine interval.\n\nFor phase advances restricted to \\([0,\\pi]\\), the monotonic arccosine transformation converts this into a certified phase interval.\n\nThis does not independently unwrap the phase or establish an absolute continuous-time frequency.
